title: When a Team Member Doesn't Prioritize Your Priorities
author: Admired Leadership Field Notes
summary: Admired Leadership takes up a frustration every leader faces: a team member follows their own priorities rather than the leader's. The piece does not assume bad intent but starts with exploratory conversation presume benign causes (competing priorities from other leaders, overload, misunderstanding). When the root cause remains opaque or the team member is unwilling to disclose it, the leader states plainly that priorities are non-negotiable and evaluation depends on accomplishing them. The leader sets timeline, names priority order, says what can be delayed, ties priorities to vision so consequences are visible, and asks what obstacles the team member is hitting. The harder conversation comes only if the pattern persists; at that point it is about the reporting line and authority structure, not the priorities themselves. The leader names the refusal plainly and offers a clear choice: accept the role or exit the team, framed by Jim Collins's line that when you feel the need to tightly manage someone, you likely have the wrong person.
points: Do not presume bad intent when a team member ignores your priorities; start with exploratory conversation to uncover competing directives, overload, or misunderstanding.
When root cause is unclear, make it clear that priorities are non-negotiable and that evaluation depends on accomplishing them; tie priorities to vision so consequences are visible.
If the pattern of misalignment persists, the conversation shifts from priorities to reporting line and authority; offer a clear choice: accept the role or exit the team.
quotes: Sometimes unknowingly and other times deliberately, team members can follow their own priorities and fail to follow yours. This can be a source of great frustration for leaders, as the work they want to get done takes a secondary position or, worse, gets ignored.
Leaders faced with the challenge of a team member who ignores their priorities are best served by initially NOT presuming bad intent.

It’s possible the team member has received competing priorities from other leaders; they are simply overloaded, and it only appears they are avoiding the priorities. Or, perhaps, they don’t understand the priority set.” “In the case where the root cause is not obvious to the team member, or they are unwilling to share it, the leader needs to make one point perfectly clear: the priorities they set are non-negotiable. This means the team member’s evaluation and success depend on their accomplishing them.
By connecting the priorities to the team’s vision, purpose, or long-range goals, the leader can further imprint the consequences of placing anything ahead of the priorities.

By plainly naming the refusal and avoiding any debate over the priorities, the leader must act decisively to define the role the team member is asked to play and to offer them a clear choice to accept the role or exit the team.
Effectiveness in anything is about doing the right things. Leaders set priorities to make the team more effective. If someone can’t or won’t align with those priorities, trust gets broken.
As author Jim Collins likes to say, “The moment you feel the need to tightly manage someone, you likely have the wrong person.” Archived from Admired Leadership on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
